newsitem.title: USA: Thousands driven from homes by North Dakota floods.
newsitem.headline: Thousands driven from homes by North Dakota floods.

text.p: The Red River, thrusting a record-high flood against miles of dikes, drove 3,000 people from their homes in Grand Forks on Friday and swamped more areas upstream in Fargo.

"This is probably a disaster of more magnitude than any of us will ever see in our lifetime," Grand Forks Mayor Pat Owens said. She ordered schools and all non-emergency businesses closed on Friday in this city of more than 70,000.

All available volunteers were asked to help fill sandbags and National Guard troops forced people in three neighbourhoods protected by weakening levees to leave their homes. Among the more than 3,000 evacuees were about 100 nursing home patients.

In Fargo, North Dakota's largest city, officials were fighting the advance of water from tributaries and melting snow in the coutryside that was moving overland toward the Red River on the city's eastern boundary.

"If I could buy two feet off the top of the river I'd spend everything I had," said Dennis Walaker, operations manager for Fargo's Public Works department. He said the overland flooding headed toward the city was something Fargo had never before faced. Earthen and sandbag dikes were being thrown up as fast as possible.
Fargo lost one skirmish with the river Thursday evening when a dike broke, flooding the Oak Grove neighbourhood. A Lutheran high school and about 20 homes were flooded.

"I looked to my right and saw that the dike was just like Jello and moving, then it gave away," said Scott Anderson who was sandbagging when the river punched through. "I didn't even look around. I just got the hell out of there."

More evacuations were under way Friday north of Moorhead, Minnesota, across the river from Fargo. Forecasters said the river was nearing a crest along a 100-mile (165-km) stretch, at a level likely to occur only once every 500 years.

Volunteers struggled throughout the night to buttress clay dikes in Grand Forks where the river hit 52.06 feet (15.87 metres) Friday, surpassing the previous record of 50 feet (15.24 metres) set in 1897. The National Weather Service said it expected the river to crest at 53 feet (16.15 metres) in Grand Forks on Friday night or early on Saturday. Flood stage in Grand Forks is 28 feet (8.5 metres).

In Fargo, where the Red hit 39.75 feet (12.12 metres) -- more than 20 feet (6.1 metres) over flood stage -- Mayor Bruce Furness said the rise appeared to be slowing. The bad news was that the river was forecast to remain at record levels for five to seven days, further straining permament and makeshift dikes.

At Grand Forks, the National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning for parts of the city. "We have no major breach in the dike at this time, but we feel they are suspect. We're doing this as a purely precautionary measure," said Byron Sieber, spokesman for the Grand Forks Emergency Operations Centre.
Sewers in some parts of Grand Forks had backed up and water was swelling through manholes in streets. Authorities pleaded with residents to limit their use of water.
The floods, unleashed by the thaw of a record winter snowfall, have covered thousands of acres in the valley of the Red River of the North along its flat and gently sloping course towards Canada.
In Ottawa, Manitoba Premier Gary Filmon said on Thursday the waters of the Red "are rapidly rising and we're expecting substantial damage and substantial cost to Manitoba."
Canadian military units were being readied for flood duty from Winnipeg southward.

North Dakota was dealing with another problem from the severe winter -- 70,000 dead cattle littering rangeland, their stiff carcasses only now poking out from melting mounds of snow. State officials said National Guard troops using earth moving equipment would be called in to dispose of the animals.
